slides.title: What Is A Container
slides.body:
Container Isolation Basics
Subheading: Process-Level Isolation
A container is a running process that shares the host machine's kernel but gets its own isolated view of files, network and other processes, with no separate guest operating system of its own.
Namespaces (covered next): limit WHAT a process can see
Control groups (covered next): limit HOW MUCH it can use
Union filesystem (covered next): layers that build the image itself
Analogy: A large building holds many separate flats: each flat has its own rooms and lock, but all share one foundation, electricity and water line — exactly as containers share one host kernel while each gets its own isolated view through namespaces.
Visual Guidance: Single host kernel box at bottom; three container boxes on top, each labelled with a small lock icon and tagged Namespaces / cgroups / Union FS.
slides.notes: Stress that isolation here is logical, enforced by the kernel, not a separate virtual hardware layer. Interviewers often ask what actually makes a container 'isolated' — the answer is these three kernel features, not a hypervisor.

slides.title: Linux Namespaces Explained
slides.body:
Linux Namespaces
Subheading: Isolating Process Views
A namespace hides a shared system resource from a process and shows it a private copy instead, so each container feels like a separate machine.
Visual Guidance: Six small labelled boxes around a central kernel icon, each box pointing to a different resource type from the table.
slides.notes: A common interview trap is confusing PID namespace isolation with resource limiting — namespaces only change what is visible, not how much can be used. Mention that chroot was an early, narrower ancestor of the mount namespace idea.
tables: Own filesystem view and mount points
Own user and group ID mapping

slides.title: Cgroups And Union Filesystem
slides.body:
Cgroups And Union FS
Subheading: Resource Limits Layers
Two more kernel features complete container isolation: control groups, known as cgroups, cap resource use, and a union filesystem builds the image itself from layers.
CPU controller: caps processor time share per group
Memory controller: breach triggers an out-of-memory kill
Block I/O controller: caps disk read and write speed
Union filesystem merges read-only layers; OverlayFS is the current standard driver
Copy-on-write duplicates a file only when it is modified
Visual Guidance: One cgroup boundary box with CPU/Memory/Disk meter icons, beside a layered stack merging into one view with a writable top layer.
slides.notes: A process crossing its memory ceiling is killed by the kernel, not slowed down. Layer caching from the union filesystem is why rebuilding an image after a small change is fast.

slides.title: Docker Architecture Overview
slides.body:
Docker Architecture Map
Subheading: Five Core Parts
Docker runs as a client-server system: a command-line client talks to a background daemon that builds and runs containers using images pulled from a registry.
Docker client — CLI issuing commands like docker run
Docker daemon (dockerd) — service building and managing containers
Images — read-only templates stored locally or in a registry
Containers — running instances created from images
Registry — remote store such as Docker Hub for images
Full installation steps and the two verification commands are covered next, on Slide 5.
Visual Guidance: Diagram: client box with arrow to daemon box; daemon connects to an images store, a container box, and a registry cloud icon.
slides.notes: Point out dockerd as the process name learners will see in ps output. Interviewers often ask to name all five Docker architecture pieces and how they interact.

slides.title: Installing And Verifying Docker
slides.body:
Docker Installation Steps
Subheading: Setup Per OS
Docker installs differently per operating system, but every path ends with the same two verification commands before any practical work begins.
docker --version
docker run hello-world
Line 1 — Confirms the client can reach a running daemon.
Line 2 — Expected: Hello from Docker! confirms the daemon pulled and ran an image.
Linux commands need a sudo prefix, for example sudo docker --version and sudo docker run hello-world.
Step 1 — Confirm WSL 2 Is Enabled (Windows)
PowerShell confirms WSL is installed/updated and the Virtual Machine Platform feature is Enabled — required before Docker Desktop will run on Windows
Step 2 — Choose Installation Options
Docker Desktop installer — Configuration screen, per-user installation with the WSL 2 backend
Step 3 — Installation Completes
Docker Desktop installer confirms “Installation succeeded”
Step 4 — Sign In Or Skip
First launch — Docker prompts to sign in or create a Docker Hub account; signing in is optional for local use and can be skipped
Step 5 — Redirected To The Desktop App
After sign-in (or skip), Docker redirects back to the desktop app
Step 6 — Confirm The Redirect
Windows asks permission to open Docker Desktop — confirms the handoff from browser back to the installed app
Step 7 — Docker Desktop Opens
Docker Desktop's Containers tab on first launch — empty, since nothing has been run yet
Step 8 — Verify From The Terminal
docker --version confirms the client is reachable; docker run hello-world confirms the daemon pulled and ran an image — “Hello from Docker!” confirms success
Visual Guidance: See the 8-step screenshot walkthrough above — Windows install path shown end to end, from enabling WSL 2 through the docker run hello-world verification.
slides.notes: Treat the final verification step as the gate before any practical work begins. A missing WSL 2 backend (Step 1) is the most common installation failure asked about. Docker Hub sign-in (Steps 4–6) is optional for local use — mention this so students don’t think an account is mandatory.
tables: Install VS Code; wsl --install; Docker Desktop (WSL 2 backend); open Docker Desktop
Install VS Code; Docker Desktop (Apple Silicon or Intel build); open Docker Desktop
Install VS Code; sudo apt install docker.io; sudo systemctl start docker

slides.title: Image vs Container Distinction
slides.body:
Image Vs Container
Subheading: Template Vs Instance
An image is a frozen, read-only template; a container is that template brought to life with its own writable layer on top.
Image: built once, never changes, stored by ID and tag
Container: created from an image, has a thin writable layer
One image can start many independent containers
Deleting a container never deletes its source image
Analogy: A cake recipe card is reused to bake many separate cakes — just as one Docker image can start many independent containers.
Visual Guidance: Side-by-side: image box with locked layers next to a container box showing the same layers plus a writable top layer.
slides.notes: Tags like nginx:alpine name images, not containers. Interviews often ask what survives container removal — the image.

slides.title: Pulling From A Registry
slides.body:
Client Daemon Registry
Subheading: Pull And Run Flow
Running an image that the daemon does not have locally triggers a pull from a registry — Docker Hub by default — before a container starts.
Explicit pull: docker pull nginx:alpine fetches an image with no container created — the same mechanism docker run triggers automatically
docker run hello-world: no flags — image name only, pulled if absent locally
Client sends the request over the daemon's local API socket
Daemon checks its local image cache first by name and tag
Pulled layers are cached, so a repeat run skips the registry
Visual Guidance: Arrow sequence: client -> daemon -> registry (dashed, only on cache miss) -> container created.
slides.notes: Explain that a one-shot container exits once its process finishes, which is normal. Interviewers often ask why a stopped container still appears in docker ps -a.

slides.title: Part A Practical Steps
slides.body:
Part A Practical Steps
Subheading: Images To Containers
Part A works with an existing image, tracing every command from an explicit pull to removing a running web server container.
Step 1: docker pull nginx:alpine fetches the image explicitly, before any container runs
Step 2: docker images lists images already pulled
Step 3: docker run hello-world; expected Hello from Docker!
Step 4: docker ps shows currently running containers
Step 5: docker ps -a shows hello-world as Exited (0)
Step 6: docker run -d --name web-demo -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine starts a server
Step 7: docker ps confirms web-demo running with its port mapping
Step 8: browser at localhost:8080 shows Welcome to nginx!
Step 9: docker stop web-demo halts the container
Step 10: docker rm web-demo removes it; docker ps -a confirms it is gone
Visual Guidance: Numbered step strip 1 to 10, icons for terminal, container box, and browser window at the matching steps.
slides.notes: This full trace is the baseline practical before the custom build in Part B. Exited (0) on hello-world is expected, not an error.

slides.title: Running A Container
slides.body:
Container Lifecycle Commands
Subheading: Run Check Stop Remove
A long-running service container is started, mapped to a host port, then checked, stopped and removed through the client-daemon flow.
Nginx is used only to demonstrate a web application running inside a container, not as a production choice.
docker run -d --name web-demo -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
Line 1 — -d: run in background. --name web-demo: name the container. -p 8080:80: map host port 8080 to container port 80. nginx:alpine: the image used.
docker images: lists cached images before running
docker ps: expected web-demo Up, PORTS 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp
Browser at port 8080: expected the Welcome to nginx! page
docker stop web-demo: expected the container name echoed back
docker rm web-demo: expected web-demo absent from docker ps -a
Browser Check — Step 8
Browser at localhost:8080 — “Welcome to nginx!” confirms web-demo is serving traffic
Visual Guidance: Timeline strip: run -> ps -> browser -> stop -> rm, each step labelled with its command. Only the browser-result screenshot above is currently available.
slides.notes: Nginx here is only a convenient web server to prove the container is serving traffic. Removing the container frees its name but the nginx:alpine image stays cached. [Instructor note: only the browser-result screenshot (Step 8) is currently available for this slide. Steps 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 and 10 still need to be captured from a live run — Step 3 (hello-world) is already shown on Slide 5 and does not need a separate capture here.]

slides.title: Layers And Build Caching
slides.body:
Layers Build Caching
Subheading: Dockerfile To Layers
Each Dockerfile instruction adds one layer on top of the base image; a rebuild reuses an unchanged layer instead of redoing its work.
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
EXPOSE 80
Line 1 — FROM sets the base layer.
Line 2 — COPY adds the HTML layer.
Line 3 — EXPOSE documents port 80, not published yet.
Cache key: instruction plus the files it touches
A changed instruction invalidates it and every layer after
Stable instructions first, frequently changing ones last
Analogy: Stacked transparency sheets — redrawing only the top sheet leaves every sheet below untouched — just as Docker reuses cached layers below an unchanged instruction.
Visual Guidance: Vertical stack of layer blocks labelled FROM, COPY, EXPOSE, with a cache tick mark on the unchanged ones.
slides.notes: EXPOSE only documents a port; -p at runtime actually publishes it. Interviews often ask why instruction order affects build speed.

slides.title: Building A Custom Image
slides.body:
Build Run Verify Subheading: Custom Image Trace Part B builds a custom image from a Dockerfile, confirming the same image-container relationship already seen with pulled images. cloud-docker-demo/ ├── index.html └── Dockerfile Lines 1-3 — A project folder holding the page content and the build instructions. My Docker App

Hello from Docker!

This web application is running inside a Docker container.

Lines 6-7 — The heading and paragraph this page serves, shown by the container once built and run. Step 1: create folder cloud-docker-demo/ with index.html and Dockerfile Step 2: write index.html with the page content above Step 3: write Dockerfile with FROM, COPY and EXPOSE Step 4: docker build -t cloud-docker-demo . builds the image Step 5: docker images confirms cloud-docker-demo stored locally Step 6: docker run -d --name cloud-web -p 8080:80 cloud-docker-demo starts it Step 7: docker ps expected cloud-web with 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp Step 8: browser at port 8080 expected the custom page Step 9: docker stop cloud-web and docker rm cloud-web remove it Step 10: docker images still lists cloud-docker-demo after removal Step 1 — Project Folder Created VS Code — cloud-docker-demo folder created in the file explorer Step 2 — index.html Written VS Code — index.html content: the custom page this container will serve Step 3 — Dockerfile Written VS Code — Dockerfile content: FROM, COPY and EXPOSE directives Step 6 — Container Started Terminal after docker run — cloud-web container ID printed Step 7 — Port Mapping Confirmed docker ps — cloud-web mapped to 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp Step 8 — Custom Page Verified Browser at localhost:8080 — the custom “Hello from Docker!” page Visual Guidance: Flow strip: Dockerfile -> docker build -> image -> docker run -> container -> browser output, matching the 6 screenshots above (Steps 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8).
slides.notes: The same build-run-remove pattern applies to any custom image. Interviews often ask which flag tags an image during build. [Instructor note: screenshots for Steps 4, 5, 9 and 10 (docker build output, docker images before and after removal, and the stop/rm confirmation) still need to be captured — not available in the current set.]

slides.title: Comparing Containers And Virtual Machines
slides.body:
Four Comparison Dimensions
Subheading: Boot Memory Size Security
Containers and virtual machines isolate workloads differently, and that difference shows up in four measurable areas before any use case is chosen.
Boot time: how quickly each starts and becomes usable
Memory footprint: RAM consumed per workload at idle
Image size and density: how many instances fit per host
Isolation strength: kernel-level sharing versus hardware-level separation
Security trade-offs: what fails if the boundary is breached
Visual Guidance: Two stacks side by side: left hardware to hypervisor to guest OS to VMs; right hardware to host OS kernel to container engine to containers.
slides.notes: Set up the four comparison dimensions before any numbers appear on the following slides. Interviewers often open this exact topic by asking for these four axes directly.

slides.title: Boot Time And Memory Footprint
slides.body:
Boot Time And Memory
Subheading: Startup Speed Compared
Starting a virtual machine boots a full guest operating system; starting a container launches one process on a kernel already running.
Cause: VM repeats bootloader, kernel init and service startup
Container skips straight to launching the application process
Lower per-instance memory lets more workloads run concurrently
Visual Guidance: Bar chart: boot time in seconds, VM bar far taller than container bar; second bar chart for idle memory, same proportion.
slides.notes: Tie the boot-time gap to the OS boot sequence, not to raw hardware speed. The seconds-versus-tens-of-seconds contrast is a standard interview comparison point.
tables: Several hundred MB to a few GB (guest OS overhead)
A few MB to tens of MB (app plus runtime)

slides.title: Image Size And Container Density
slides.body:
Image Size Density
Subheading: Packing Workloads Tighter
Image size sets how many workload copies fit on one host, so container images routinely pack far denser than VM images.
Smaller images pull and deploy faster across a cluster
Higher density lowers infrastructure cost per workload on identical hardware
Shared base layers cut total storage across many container images
Visual Guidance: Grid diagram: one host square packed with few large VM blocks versus the same size host packed with many small container blocks.
slides.notes: Density is the number behind why a host runs far more containers than VMs side by side. Expect a question on why container density beats VM density on identical hardware.
tables: Several GB (full guest OS plus app)
Tens of MB to a few hundred MB (app layers only)

slides.title: Isolation Strength Containers Versus VMs
slides.body:
Isolation Strength Compared
Subheading: Kernel Versus Hardware
A virtual machine isolates at the hardware boundary with its own kernel; a container isolates at the process boundary on one shared kernel.
VM: separate guest kernel per instance, hypervisor enforces the boundary
Container: namespaces separate the view, cgroups cap the resources
Shared kernel means one kernel vulnerability can reach every container
VM isolation survives a single guest crash without affecting siblings
Visual Guidance: Boundary diagram: VM boundary drawn around hardware layer (per guest); container boundary drawn around process layer (one shared kernel line beneath all).
slides.notes: This single fact explains why containers are called less isolated than VMs — shared kernel, not weaker code. Interviewers test this by asking what a kernel exploit can reach in each model.

slides.title: Security Trade-offs Between Containers And VMs
slides.body:
Security Trade-offs
Subheading: Blast Radius Differs
Stronger isolation does not mean fewer attacks; it changes how far a successful attack can spread once the boundary is crossed.
VM breakout needs a hypervisor flaw: rare, high severity
Container breakout exploits the shared kernel: mitigated by seccomp, SELinux, non-root users
Untrusted or multi-tenant code favours VM-grade isolation
Trusted internal services accept container isolation for speed and density
Visual Guidance: Two circles labelled blast radius: small circle around one VM after a breakout, large circle around the whole host after a container breakout.
slides.notes: Link blast radius back to the kernel-sharing fact from the isolation comparison just taught. This security-versus-density trade-off is a frequent systems-design interview question.

slides.title: Choosing Containers Or VMs
slides.body:
Choosing Between Them
Subheading: Use Cases And Criteria
Container and virtual machine strengths point to different workloads; matching the right one to the job is the real skill, not finding one universal winner.
Workload type: stateless microservices vs full-stack legacy apps
Isolation need: process-level sharing vs hardware-level separation
OS requirement: same kernel vs mixed operating systems
Scale and density: many light instances vs fewer, heavier ones
Visual Guidance: Diagram: a fork from one question mark — left arrow to a container icon tagged with workload types, right arrow to a VM icon tagged with workload types.
slides.notes: Frame this as a workload-driven decision rather than a technology preference, since that is the real trade-off teams make daily. This exact mapping is what interviewers probe when testing container-versus-VM judgment.

slides.title: Container Use Cases
slides.body:
Container Use Cases
Subheading: Where Containers Fit Best
Containers suit workloads that restart often, scale horizontally, and ship as small, repeatable units — the opposite of a slow-booting, heavyweight guest.
Microservices: independently deployable services communicating over APIs
CI/CD pipelines: identical images carried from build to production
Cloud-native apps: run at scale on AWS ECS, EKS or Fargate
Stateless, short-lived tasks: batch jobs and queue workers
High-density hosting: many app instances packed onto one host
Visual Guidance: Row of icons: microservice mesh, CI/CD pipeline arrow, ECS/EKS logo, batch-job icon, stacked boxes for density.
slides.notes: Tie each case back to the density and startup-speed advantages already established, applied here to real workload choices. Expect interview questions phrased as which workload suits a container — these five cases are the answer key.

slides.title: Virtual Machine Use Cases
slides.body:
VM Use Cases
Subheading: Where VMs Fit Best
Virtual machines earn their heavier footprint when a workload needs a full, isolated operating system or hardware access the host runtime cannot provide.
Legacy applications: tied to a specific OS version or kernel module
Mixed operating systems: Windows and Linux guests on one host
Strong multi-tenant isolation: separate kernels for untrusted workloads
Kernel-level or driver work: needs direct hardware or kernel access
Full-stack test labs: AWS EC2 instances cloning a production server exactly
Visual Guidance: Icons: Windows and Linux logos side by side, a lock for isolation, EC2 logo for the test-lab case.
slides.notes: Connect each case back to the full-OS isolation and boot-time cost already established, now framed as the reason to choose a VM. A classic interview probe asks why not containerise everything — kernel dependency and tenant isolation are the answer.

slides.title: Decision Criteria Compared
slides.body:
Decision Criteria Map
Subheading: Workload Fit Checklist
No single criterion decides the choice; the table weighs isolation, OS diversity, density and workload lifetime side by side.
Production systems often combine both — containers scheduled onto VM-based hosts — using the VM as the security boundary and containers for density within it.
Visual Guidance: Keep the table as the slide centrepiece; below it, a small nested box showing container icons inside one VM icon to depict the hybrid pattern.
slides.notes: Use this table as a quick checklist when justifying an architecture choice, since most real decisions weigh several rows together. Interview panels often ask for a one-line justification per row, which this table trains directly.
tables: Multiple OS types on one host

slides.title: Virtualization And Container Tooling Overview
slides.body:
Tooling Landscape
Subheading: Four Areas Mapped
Running virtual machines or containers in production means picking a hypervisor or engine, then a registry to distribute the resulting images.
Virtualization tools: VirtualBox, KVM, Hyper-V, VMware
Container engines: Docker, Podman, containerd
Registries: public vs private
Tagging: naming scheme for image versions
Visual Guidance: Two-column diagram: VM tools column, container tools column, both arrows pointing down into one shared Registry box.
slides.notes: Set up these four areas before going tool by tool. Interviewers often ask for alternatives to Docker or VirtualBox by name.

slides.title: Comparing VirtualBox, KVM, Hyper-V And VMware
slides.body:
VM Tooling Compared
Subheading: Four Hypervisor Products
Each virtualization product fits a different deployment, from a laptop test lab to a production data centre.
Visual Guidance: Four-row table, one small vendor logo icon beside each tool name.
slides.notes: Tie each product back to the Type 1 versus Type 2 split already taught. Interviewers often ask which hypervisor backs a named cloud platform.

slides.title: Containerd And Podman Beneath Docker
slides.body:
Beneath Docker's Daemon
Subheading: Containerd And Podman
Docker's own daemon delegates actual container execution to containerd, a lower-level runtime that Kubernetes also calls directly, bypassing Docker entirely.
containerd: split out of Docker in 2016, now a separate project
containerd runs the OCI Runtime Spec through runc underneath
Podman removes the central daemon altogether; each container is a direct process
Podman's rootless mode starts containers without any root privilege
Analogy: A city bus needs a central depot dispatching every trip, while an auto-rickshaw driver picks up a passenger directly with no depot involved — exactly as Podman starts a container directly, with no daemon standing between the command and the running process.
Visual Guidance: Diagram: Docker box with arrow down to containerd box; separate Podman box with no daemon, arrow straight to container.
slides.notes: Containerd living inside Docker, and now also standalone, is a common interview trick question. Note that Podman's daemonless design is the security motivation, not a performance one.

slides.title: Docker Vs Podman Vs Containerd
slides.body:
Engines Compared
Subheading: Architecture And Role
The three tools sit at different layers of one stack, and that layering decides which one fits a given deployment.
Visual Guidance: Four-row comparison table, highlight the Primary Role row in a contrasting colour.
slides.notes: This table is the one most asked about in container-tooling interviews. Stress that containerd, not Docker, is the runtime a Kubernetes node actually calls.

slides.title: Public Vs Private Container Registries
slides.body:
Public Vs Private
Subheading: Image Registries
A registry stores and distributes container images; which kind is used decides who is able to pull a given image.
Public registry: Docker Hub, open to any pull request
Private registry: Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry
Self-hosted option: Harbor, run inside an organisation's own network
Chosen for security, compliance or protecting proprietary images
Analogy: A public registry is like a library open to any visitor, while a private registry is like an office cupboard that opens only with an employee's key — exactly as a private registry demands authentication before an image can be pulled.
Visual Guidance: Split diagram: public registry with an open padlock icon, private registry with a closed padlock, both feeding a docker pull arrow.
slides.notes: Distinguish a registry, the service, from a repository, one image's set of tags, if asked in an interview. Private registries are the default choice for any proprietary production image.

slides.title: Tagging Strategy For Container Images
slides.body:
Tagging Strategy
Subheading: Naming Image Versions
Every image push attaches a tag, and the tag chosen decides whether that exact build can be found and redeployed later.
Semantic versioning: major.minor.patch, for example app:2.3.1
latest tag: moves with every push, unsafe for production rollback
Immutable tag: git-commit hash, for example app:a1b2c3d, never overwritten
Environment tags: app:staging, app:prod mark the pipeline stage
Visual Guidance: Timeline of three pushes to one repository, each landing a different immutable tag, with the latest pointer jumping between them.
slides.notes:
Flag latest as the most common cause of a failed production rollback when this comes up in interviews. Immutable, hash-based tags are what real CI/CD pipelines rely on for traceability.
Heads-Up: Start Your AWS Account Setup Now
Why now: Lab L1 (Working with Docker Images and Containers), conducted right after this session, needs a working AWS account to launch an EC2 instance — account creation and identity verification can take a day or more to clear.
Create the AWS account before the next session, not the morning of the lab
Identity and payment verification can take time to process — this is the usual delay, not an error
A free-tier account is sufficient for L1; no charges are expected if usage stays within free-tier limits

slides.title: Key Takeaways
slides.body:
1. Container Fundamentals: Process-level isolation; Linux namespaces & control groups (cgroups); union filesystem & layered images
2. Docker Architecture: Client, daemon, images, containers & registries; image vs container; layers & build caching
3. Containers vs VMs: Boot time, memory footprint, image size & density; isolation strength & security trade-offs
4. Choosing Between Them: Container use cases; VM use cases; decision criteria
5. Tooling & Registries: VirtualBox, KVM, Hyper-V & VMware; Docker, Podman & containerd; public vs private registries; tagging strategy
